summary: Aims to focus discussion on authentication problems in the Internet and possible solutions. It suggests mediated access-control and authentication procedures for setting up an association between users in different trust environments. The proposals were experimental and not intended as standards.

plainLanguage.summary: When two strangers need to trust each other, a friend that both know can vouch for them. This memo suggests using that kind of middleman for computers.

questions: how to authenticate users across trust domains
what is the distributed-protocol authentication scheme
how does cookie jar authentication work
what is the difference between cookie jar and needham-schroeder
subtitle: Secure authentication across different network trust domains using a trusted server.

tldr.problem: When distributed gateway protocols like EGP need to authenticate each other across different trust domains, they need a way to verify identities without pre-shared secrets, while resisting spoofing and replay attacks.
tldr.mechanism: A trusted Cookie Jar server assigns each requesting user a one-time random session key. Users encrypt their checksums with that key and send them to their peer, proving they obtained the key from the trusted server and preventing reply attacks.
tldr.outcome: The scheme was experimental and never standardized. It influenced later thinking about authentication but was not widely deployed in EGP or other gateway protocols.

facts.label: Message ID
facts.value: Random initial, then incremented per message

today: RFC 1004 is an Experimental document that was never standardized. While it contributed ideas about authentication in distributed protocols, it was not widely adopted for EGP, DGP, or other systems. It remains a historical example of 1980s thinking about network authentication and trust.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1004 proposes distributed-protocol authentication, a scheme for authenticating associations between users in different trust environments using a trusted Cookie Jar server. The RFC aims to focus discussion on authentication problems in Internet distributed protocols like the Exterior Gateway Protocol (EGP) and the proposed Dissimilar Gateway Protocol (DGP), rather than to establish standards.

An association is an end-to-end path between two users (peers) where the users themselves are trusted, but the network between them is not. The network may drop, duplicate, or corrupt messages. A hostile attacker on the network might intercept, modify, and retransmit messages. The Cookie Jar scheme uses cryptographic checksums and encryption to authenticate messages, proving that only the intended sender could have generated them, and preventing replayed messages from earlier associations.
sections.plainLanguage: Two peers need to trust each other over an untrusted network. A trusted third party (the Cookie Jar) helps them prove they are who they say they are.

sections.title: Trust Model and Concepts
sections.content:
Each user is assigned a public address (like an autonomous system identifier, an Internet address, or a name) and a private key known only to the user and the Cookie Jar. A public directory lists each user's address and its access-control list (who it is permitted to associate with), but the private key is never disclosed.

An association between two users i and j is identified by the combination of both addresses and a one-time session key K(i,j) generated by the Cookie Jar. This key is generated fresh for each new association; no caching or key reuse is allowed. The Cookie Jar maintains a private table of [user address, private key] pairs for all sanctioned users and uses the public access-control lists to authorize requests.

The scheme distinguishes between the association from i to j and the reciprocal from j to i by which user requests the Cookie Jar first. Once an association begins, all previous state is erased: if either user crashes, loses connectivity, or requests a new association, they must go through the full procedure again.
sections.plainLanguage: Each person has a secret key nobody knows except the banker. A list on the wall says who is allowed to do business with whom. When two people want to associate, the banker creates a new secret code just for them.

sections.title: Authentication Procedure
sections.content:
The Cookie Jar scheme uses a five-step procedure. Step 1: Requestor i rolls a random message ID and sends it with the association specifier [A(i), A(j)] as a request to the Cookie Jar. Step 2: The Cookie Jar checks the access-control list; if the association is valid, it generates a random session key K(i,j) and returns two encrypted cookies: one for i (encrypted with i's private key) and one for j (encrypted first with j's private key, then with i's). Step 3: Requestor i decrypts the cookies with its key, verifies the checksum, and passes the encrypted j cookie to user j along with a fresh message ID and the checksum, all encrypted with the session key K(i,j). Step 4: User j decrypts the i cookie, uses it to verify the message ID checksum with the session key, and returns a confirmation message with its own initial message ID, also encrypted with K(i,j). Step 5: All subsequent messages increment the message ID, recompute the checksum, and encrypt the message ID fields with K(i,j). Receivers decrypt with K(i,j), verify the checksum, and discard messages with invalid checksums or out-of-order sequence numbers.

The checksum is computed using the Internet checksum algorithm (ones-complement sum) over all message bits including addresses and sequence numbers. The encrypted fields are encrypted with DES (Data Encryption Standard).
sections.plainLanguage: First, i asks the banker for a code. The banker checks the rulebook and gives i a secret code for j. Then i sends j an encrypted message with that code. J decrypts it, proves it is from the banker, and sends back its own encrypted message. After that, they keep encrypting messages with the secret code.

sections.title: Security Properties and Limitations
sections.content:
The scheme protects against several attacks. If an attacker intercepts and modifies a message without knowing the session key K(i,j), the checksum will fail and the message is discarded. If an attacker tries to impersonate user i in a replay of the Cookie Jar reply, the message will fail the checksum test because it is missing the knowledge of j's private key. The use of message IDs and sequence numbers prevents replays of later messages.

However, the RFC acknowledges vulnerabilities. The Internet checksum algorithm has known weaknesses: it is invariant to word order and byte swap, and the checksum field is only 16 bits, so an attacker might brute-force all possible checksums. Additionally, an attacker might stockpile intercepted message 3 (the requestor's initial association message) and replay it at speed to cause denial of service by triggering repeated timeouts, even if the attacks do not succeed in establishing a working association. The RFC argues that adding a three-way handshake (as in the Needham-Schroeder scheme) would not solve this because an attacker can still induce the same performance signature as network loss.

The scheme does not encrypt the data payload itself, only the checksum and sequence number. It is designed to authenticate messages against spoofing and replay, not to hide data transmission.
sections.plainLanguage: If someone tries to fake a message, the checksum will not match and it gets thrown away. But someone could try a lot of replayed old messages to cause trouble. The RFC admits the checksum is not super strong, but says that even better checksums would not help against someone who just floods with old messages.

sections.title: Application to Gateway Protocols
sections.content:
The RFC proposes incorporating the scheme into EGP and DGP by adding the Cookie Jar fields to their existing Request and Confirm messages. In DGP, a Request command from one peer causes both peers to reinitialize all state and send a Confirm response, similar to other protocols. The Request operation involves first requesting a key from the Cookie Jar (the first two messages), then sending the actual Request command (message 3 in the scheme above).

Since the Request command and all subsequent messages use the keys from the Cookie Jar, any message with an invalid checksum is discarded. If either peer loses state (due to a crash, for example), it will not recognize subsequent messages and will eventually timeout, at which point it or its peer reinitates the procedure.

The RFC notes that if both peers attempt to authenticate at the same time, their authentication sequences may cross in the network. Since the Request message is self-authenticating, whichever Request arrives first will reset the keys. The peer expecting the earlier Confirm response will discard it as invalid and retry after timeout, effectively using staggered timeouts to break the race condition.
sections.plainLanguage: When two gateways want to talk to each other, they add the Cookie Jar steps to their normal neighbor-acquisition handshake. If a gateway crashes, it will not understand the other's messages and will wait for a timeout, then ask for a new secret code.
